name: Breton

ancestors.notes: Descent from Common Brythonic via insular settlers
French adstrate: heavy lexical and phonological influence
Gaulish substrate traces in Armorican territory

notes: Breton (Brezhoneg). ~200,000 speakers (est. 2020). Brittany, France. Brought from Britain by insular Brythonic speakers (~5th–6th c. CE). Four main dialects: Léonard (KLT basis), Trégorrois, Cornouaillais, Vannetais (most divergent). INPUT CONTRACT: peurunvan (the 1941 "wholly unified" orthography), which is what ⟨zh⟩, ⟨c'h⟩ and the plural digraph ⟨où⟩ identify; the interdialectal and skolveurieg systems spell the same words differently and are not this spec's input. The pronunciation described is the KLT-based standard: ⟨zh⟩ = /z/ (it is /h/ in Vannetais), ⟨c'h⟩ = /x/, penultimate stress. ⟨c'h⟩ is also written with U+2019 and U+02BC in running text, so all three apostrophes are mapped — an unmapped one silently deletes the ⟨c⟩ and leaves ⟨h⟩. French strongly influenced phonology (uvular /ʁ/, nasal vowels in loans). Refs: Hemon (1975), Press (1986), Hewitt (1978).

sources.notes: Penultimate (paroxytone) word stress in KLT and the standard against final stress in Vannetais, after ALBB map 506 and Falc'hun (1947).

stress.notes: KLT and the standard are paroxytone; Vannetais is oxytone. ARBRES (Jouitteau, ed.), 'Accentuation', 'Mots simples': "Le KLT accentue sur l'avant-dernière syllabe (paroxyton ...), quand le vannetais accentue sur la dernière (oxyton)", after ALBB map 506. This spec describes the KLT-based standard, so -2; a Gwenedeg spec would set -1. ⟨y⟩ and ⟨w⟩ spell /j/ and /w/ and are never nuclei, so vowel_letters is declared rather than left to the cross-linguistic letter-shape test.

allophone_rules.notes: Hewitt (1978), Journal of the International Phonetic Association 8(1-2):80, doi:10.1017/S0025100300001766: "Stress is strong. Unstressed vowels are short, stressed vowels are half long unless before fortis (voiceless, double) consonants or consonant clusters, where they are short." Stated positively: the lengthening context is a single lenis consonant, so followed_by_phoneme names the lenis series and followed_by_2 requires a vowel two slots on — which is what makes the consonant single rather than the first member of a cluster. The condition is stated on the UNDERLYING phoneme, so ⟨Gwened⟩ lengthens before the /d/ that BR_FINAL_DEVOICE_D later realises as [t]. A monosyllable closed by a single lenis consonant (⟨bazh⟩, ⟨chug⟩) has no vowel two slots on and so is left short here; that context is not described by this rule.

Hewitt (1978), Journal of the International Phonetic Association 8(1-2):80, doi:10.1017/S0025100300001766: "Stress is strong. Unstressed vowels are short, stressed vowels are half long unless before fortis (voiceless, double) consonants or consonant clusters, where they are short." A word-final stressed vowel stands before no consonant at all, so it is inside the lengthening context: ⟨du⟩ [dyː], ⟨re⟩ [ʁeː], ⟨bro⟩ [bʁoː].

Hewitt (1978), JIPA 8(1-2):80, doi:10.1017/S0025100300001766, records "lenis obstruent devoicing in final pausal position and in sandhi". Peurunvan writes the lenis member (⟨z zh d g b j⟩) and leaves the alternation unwritten, so it is stated here and not in the grapheme table. ⟨Breizh⟩ [bʁɛjs], ⟨Pariz⟩ [paːʁis].
